 JUDGMENT

The present appeal is directed against the order dated 15.05.2025 passed by the Learned V Metropolitan Magistrate & Traffic Court, Bengaluru in Crl. Misc. No. 23/2024, whereby the petition filed by the appellants under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act,
2005 came to be dismissed for default.

sentences.text: The petitioner in Crl.Misc.23/2024 before the trial court having preferred the instant appeal against the respondent.

The appellant and respondent are hereby assigned with their original ranks before the trial court i.e., the appellant as petitioner and respondent as respondent in the instant discussion for the purpose of brevity and convenience to avoid the confusion and perplexity.

3. The Appellant No.1 and the Respondent are Hindus by religion, whose marriage was solemnised with due observance of Hindu rites and ceremonies on 28.09.2014 at Palace Sheesh Mahal, Palace Grounds, Sri Ramana Maharshi Road, Bengaluru.

Their marital union was subsequently registered on 24.12.2016 under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, before the Registrar of Marriages, Shivajinagar,
Bengaluru, vide CD No. SHVM22, Marriage Registration No. SHV-HM130-2016-17.

From this wedlock, a female child, Miss Kiara Menon (Appellant No.2), was born on 30.12.2016, who is presently aged 8 years and is pursuing her education in Grade III at The Brigade School, Whitefield,
Bengaluru.

Since birth, the minor child has been in the exclusive care and custody of her mother, the Appellant No.1.
4.
The Appellant No.1 has been subjected to a continuous course of physical, emotional, and psychological cruelty, both during and after pregnancy.

It is specifically alleged that on 04.01.2024,
the Respondent committed an act of physical assault upon the Appellant No.1 in the presence of their minor daughter, following which he deserted the matrimonial home.

These acts, coupled with repeated instances of verbal abuse, financial abandonment, mental harassment, postpartum neglect,
and derisive commentary, have compelled the Appellants to initiate proceedings under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

In support of these allegations, a complaint was also preferred by the Appellant No.1 before the High Grounds Police Station,
resulting in registration of FIR in Crime No. 0008/2024 under Sections 323, 498A, and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, culminating into C.C. No. 13713/2024, which is presently pending adjudication before the Court of the Learned I Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bengaluru.

5. In addition to the aforementioned criminal case, the Appellant No.1 has initiated a petition under Sections 7, 17, and 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, in G & WC No. 12/2024 seeking permanent custody and consequential reliefs, and another petition under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 seeking dissolution of marriage on grounds of cruelty, both of which are pending before the Hon'ble V Additional Principal Judge, Family Court, Bengaluru.

During the pendency of the Domestic Violence Petition, the Learned Trial Court was pleased to grant an ex Ashwini Kovithila Thaze Veedu vs Aditya Menon on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/35769450/

sentences.text: However, the said protection order was vacated vide subsequent order dated 26.07.2024, upon application by the Respondent, thereby depriving the Appellants of both monetary support and protective restraint.
6. Subsequent to the vacation of interim reliefs, the Appellant No.1 was left solely responsible for the entire financial burden, including legal fees and child-rearing expenses.

While the Appellants sought and obtained a final opportunity to lead evidence on 07.12.2024 after engaging new counsel, the period witnessed several settlement overtures from the Respondent's side, prompting adjournments based on verbal assurances communicated through counsel.
Despite such bona fide participation in settlement discussions, the Appellant was unable to appear before the Trial Court on 17.04.2025 due to sudden illness.

The matter was eventually listed on 15.05.2025 before an in-charge court, which,
without due consideration of the surrounding facts or granting a reasonable opportunity, proceeded to dismiss the petition for default.

The impugned dismissal order, passed without recording sufficient or cogent reasons, has caused grave prejudice to the Appellants, particularly in light of the continuing nature of domestic violence and the statutory mandate to protect the rights of aggrieved women and minor children under the PWDV Act.
7. Being aggrieved by the impugned order Dated; 15.5.2025 the appellant/ petitioner before the trial court, has filed this appeal on the following among the other grounds.

GROUNDS OF APPEAL a) The Appellant respectfully submits that the impugned order dated 15.05.2025 passed by the Trial Court, in Criminal Misc. No. 23/2024, dismissing the Petition is unsustainable in law and on facts and is liable to be set aside for the following, amongst other grounds, each of which is taken without prejudice to the others:
b) That the impugned order is arbitrary and passed in a mechanical manner, without application of judicial mind.

c) The Trial Court has failed to assess the circumstances surrounding adjournments in the context of ongoing settlement discussions: The Appellant No.1 and her counsel met at the office of the Respondent's counsel to discuss settlement talks, and upon the insistence of the Respondent's counsel for a mutual settlement out of court, the Appellants were precluded from conducting the proceedings before the Trial Court.
d) At this juncture that the Respondent approached appellant No.1 through his counsel with a proposal for amicable settlement.
In furtherance of this, draft settlement agreements were also exchanged between the parties.

Proposed settlement agreements were sent by the Respondent Counsel on 07.02.2025,
18.02.2025, 24.02.2025 and 14.03.2025.

On 14.03.2025, the Respondent's counsel while sharing the draft settlement agreement stated that should the Appellants not Ashwini Kovithila Thaze Veedu vs Aditya Menon on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/35769450/
3 agree to the terms therein, then the matter can proceed.
e) On multiple occasions, the Respondent and his legal counsel made oral representations requesting Appellant No.1 to refrain from actively pursuing the proceedings, assuring that the matter would be settled out of court.

sentences.text: Relying on the bona fide premise of a possible resolution and in the interest of avoiding prolonged litigation, the Appellants instructed their counsel accordingly and refrained from leading evidence all the while reciprocating to the settlement talks.
f) However, in spite of repeatedly trying, all talks of settlement failed between the parties.

Upon the breakdown of the settlement discussions between the parties, and in the absence of any concrete or bona fide effort on the part of the Respondent to amicably resolve the dispute, the Appellants were left with no alternative but to resume and diligently pursue the legal proceedings before the concerned Trial Courts.
However, on 29.03.2025, since the Trial court was not in session on account of the Presiding Officer being transferred, the matter was adjourned in the same stage.
Hence, the Trial Court erred in dismissing the Petition solely on the ground that 11 adjournments had been sought to adduce evidence, without examining the reasons for those adjournments.

The Trial Court failed to appreciate that the adjournments were not sought with the intent to delay proceedings but were occasioned by genuine circumstances, including the pendency of settlement discussions between the parties in all the connected matrimonial proceedings.
g) Trial Court has failed to appreciate that the counsel was present on all the hearing dates: The appellants through their counsel, have diligently appeared before the trial Court on all previous hearing dates.
On each occasion where an adjournment was sought the factual difficulties faced by appellant No.1 including the on-going settlement talks with the Respondent were duly explained to the Court.
Only upon such explanation being tendered and found to be bona-fide was the matter adjourned in the same stage.
At no point was there any wilful default or negligence on the part of the Appellants in conducting the matter.
The Trial Court has failed to consider the overall conduct of the appellant who has been diligently prosecuting the matter, and the surrounding circumstances.

On the date of the Impugned Order being passed, the Counsel on record for the Appellants had inadvertently noted down the wrong date and could not appear when the matter was taken up, this was the only occasion on which the Appellant counsel could not be present before the Trial Court.
The party must not be penalized or suffer due to the fault of the advocate.
Hence, the Impugned Order is liable to be set aside.

h) The Trial Court has failed to consider that, parallelly the connected proceedings were being contested aggressively by both the parties (G&WC No. 12 of 2024), the Respondent's counsel has misled the in- charge judge of the Trial Court to believe that the Appellant is not interested in leading evidence and pursuing the matter further.

Appellant No.1 is single-handedly bearing the entire responsibility of nurturing and providing for the minor daughter, without any support,
financial or otherwise, from the Respondent.
The Respondent's continued non

-cooperation in matters concerning the child compelled the Appellant to approach the Family Court even for routine and necessary decisions, such as changing the school of the minor daughter and change of place of residence of the Appellant No.1 and 2.

The requirement of seeking judicial Intervention for such day- to-day matters added an undue burden upon the Appellant, both emotionally and logistically,

l) The impugned order has the effect of denying the Appellant her right to be heard and to seek protection under law, and therefore warrants interference and setting aside by this Hon'ble Court.
The Appellants had sought urgent reliefs before the Trial Court in the nature of a protection order under Section 18 of the PWDV Act to prevent the Respondent from entering the residence of Appellant No.1 and from visiting the minor child's school, owing to his aggressive and intimidating behaviour.
It is relevant to note that, IA No. 3 (seeking return of stridhan, (compensation of INR 1 crore were also pending adjudication before the Trial Court at the time of passing of the Impugned Order.

m) The Trial Court ought to have considered that a more appropriate course would have been to impose costs or grant a final opportunity and post the matter to the very next day, rather than an outright dismissal of the petition for default at 12:45PM, which has caused grave prejudice to the Petitioner.

The in-charge judge of the Trial Court, without examining the surrounding circumstances in their entirety, and solely relying on the one-sided submissions of the Respondent's counsel, proceeded to pass the Impugned Order.
A mere perusal of the order sheet of the number of adjournments granted could not have provided the entire facts, circumstances and ongoing developments in the entire matrimonial proceedings.
Crucially, on an earlier date when adjournment had been sought due to settlement discussions between the parties, a request was made by the Appellants' counsel to record the same in the order sheet.
However, the regular Presiding Officer of the Trial Court orally indicated that since the discussions were being held "out of court," he was not inclined to record such a reason.

As a result, these developments, which are central to understanding the conduct of the Appellants, could not have been properly appreciated by the in-charge judge of the Trial Court before whom the matter was taken up on 15.05.2025, who dismissed the Petition for default in haste at 12:45PM.

Even assuming there was some delay, the Trial Court could have exercised its discretion more judiciously by issuing a final warning or granting a last opportunity to lead evidence.
Instead, the in-charge Presiding Officer proceeded to dismiss the petition in default in a mechanical manner, without affording a proper opportunity to be heard.

The Trial Court thus failed to properly exercise its discretion and to consider the totality of circumstances, including the bona reasons for previous adjournments and the Appellants' continued participation in related proceedings.
This has resulted in manifest prejudice to the Appellants and has caused a grave miscarriage of justice.
Hence, the Impugned Order is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice and equity.
n) In view of the foregoing, it is imperative for the Appellants to be permitted to continue prosecuting the Petition before the Trial Court.

The Impugned Order dismissing the Petition for default, without duly appreciating the bona-fide difficulties faced by the Appellants, has caused grave prejudice to their rights and remedies under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

r) That the Impugned Order amounts to a miscarriage of justice and must be set aside in the interest of equity, fairness, and the rule of law.

The impugned order, therefore, deserves to be set aside.

Hence, the Appellant / petitioners pray before this Court to set aside the impugned order dated 15.5.2025 in Crl.Misc.23/2024 passed by the V Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Bengaluru and restore the proceedings to its original place i.e., before the trial court in Crl.Misc.23/2024 by allowing this Criminal Appeal in the interest of justice and equity.

8. The respondent has filed detailed written arguments opposing the appeal, asserting that the order of dismissal is justified and that the appellants were consistently negligent and disinterested in leading evidence despite repeated opportunities.

FIR registered in Crime No. 0008/2024 under Sections 323, 498A, 506 IPC; charge sheet filed in C.C. No. 13713/2024.
Proceedings also pending under the Guardian and Wards Act and under the Hindu Marriage Act.
In the DV proceedings, interim relief was initially granted on 09.02.2024 but later vacated on 26.07.2024.
Petition thereafter posted for evidence; adjournments sought, settlement talks attempted, counsel changed, illness cited.
On 15.05.2025, the in-charge court dismissed the petition for default at 12:45 PM, citing repeated failure to lead evidence.

9. In light of the rival contentions, the following pivotal points emerge for determination in this appeal:
1.
Whether the Trial Court was justified in dismissing the petition for default on 15.05.2025?
2. Whether the appellants have shown sufficient and bona fide reasons for their inability to lead evidence despite adjournments?
3. Whether the dismissal order frustrates the object of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005?

sentences.text: 4. What order?
At first blush, this appears to be a justifiable conclusion since repeated adjournments dilute the efficacy of proceedings.

12. The Respondent's counsel has rightly relied on Shiv Cotex v. Tirgun Auto Plast Pvt. Ltd., (2011) 9 SCC 678, where the Hon'ble Supreme Court cautioned against granting adjournments in a routine and mechanical manner.

entities.text: Shiv Cotex v. Tirgun Auto Plast Pvt. Ltd., (2011) 9 SCC 678
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Court observed that misplaced sympathy towards dilatory litigants erodes public confidence in the justice delivery system.
13. However, the principle laid down therein is not to be applied in isolation or divorced from the facts of each case.

In the present matter, the appellants have pointed out genuine circumstances--illness, settlement talks, change of counsel, and parallel custody litigation--which Ashwini Kovithila Thaze Veedu vs Aditya Menon on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/35769450/
7

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: ought to have been considered by the Magistrate before resorting to dismissal.
14. In Kailash v. Nanhku, (2005) 4 SCC 480, the Supreme Court held that rules of procedure are handmaids of justice and should not be construed to defeat substantive rights.
The same approach must be adopted here, particularly when rights under a beneficial legislation are at stake.
15. Thus, while the Trial Court was right in being concerned with repeated adjournments, it fell into error by failing to balance procedural discipline with substantive justice.

16. The respondent has argued, relying on S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, (1994) 1 SCC 1,
that the appellants approached the court with unclean hands, having made contradictory statements regarding settlement and reasons for absence.

entities.text: S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, (1994) 1 SCC 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 17. While this Court agrees that litigants must approach courts with candour, the peculiar stress and multiplicity of matrimonial disputes must be kept in mind.

In Rafiq v. Munshilal, (1981) 2 SCC 788,
the Supreme Court held that a party should not be penalised for the mistake of counsel, recognizing the inequity of punishing the client for no fault of their own.
18. Here, on 15.05.2025, the petition was dismissed when the matter was called out at 12:45 PM.

The explanation offered--that counsel noted a wrong date and that the appellant was medically unfit on an earlier date-- cannot be brushed aside as mala fide without deeper scrutiny.
19.

The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Smt. Shakuntala v. State of Karnataka, 2020 SCC OnLine Kar 173, held that in sensitive matters involving domestic violence, courts must adopt a liberal approach while dealing with procedural lapses, to ensure that substantive rights of women and children are not defeated.

entities.text: Smt. Shakuntala v. State of Karnataka, 2020 SCC OnLine Kar 173
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 20. The reasons cited by the appellants--settlement negotiations, illness, logistical difficulties--though imperfect, appear bona fide and consistent with the realities of protracted family litigation.
21. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is remedial and protective in nature.

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: In V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot, (2012) 3 SCC 183, the Supreme Court underscored that the Act was enacted to provide immediate relief to women subjected to violence, and therefore must be interpreted purposively.

entities.text: V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot, (2012) 3 SCC 183
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
22. The dismissal of a DV petition for default, particularly where applications for protection,
maintenance, and compensation were pending, defeats the legislative intent.
It effectively renders the victim without remedy and emboldens the alleged aggressor.
23. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma, (2013) 15 SCC 755, emphasized that courts must interpret the DV Act liberally to extend maximum protection to aggrieved women.

entities.text: Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma, (2013) 15 SCC 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A mechanical dismissal on the ground of adjournments undermines this protective mandate.

25. The respondent has contended that the appellants deliberately suppressed facts and prolonged proceedings, and therefore deserve no indulgence.

Reliance was placed on Dalip Singh v. State of U.P., (2010) 2 SCC 114, wherein the Court lamented the rise of litigants approaching courts with unclean hands.
26.

entities.text: Dalip Singh v. State of U.P., (2010) 2 SCC 114
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This Court is mindful of the principle that litigants must act fairly.
However, unlike in Dalip Singh, the present case involves allegations of domestic violence affecting a minor child and a mother.
The equities here demand a different balancing exercise.
27. Even assuming that there were contradictions in the appellants' explanations, outright dismissal of the petition is disproportionate.
A more appropriate course would have been to impose costs or grant a peremptory last opportunity.

28. In N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, (1998) 7 SCC 123, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that courts should adopt a justice-oriented approach in condoning lapses, provided there is no mala fide intent.

entities.text: N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, (1998) 7 SCC 123
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The ratio is squarely applicable here.
29. Thus, while the respondent's grievance regarding delay is noted, the remedy lies not in dismissal, but in regulating the proceedings with strict timelines and conditions.
30. The doctrine of proportionality requires that judicial discretion be exercised in a manner that is fair, just, and not excessive.
In Om Prakash v. State of Jharkhand, (2012) 12 SCC 72, Hon'ble Supreme Court reiterated that the exercise of judicial discretion must be tempered with proportionality.

entities.text: Om Prakash v. State of Jharkhand, (2012) 12 SCC 72
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 31. Here, the Magistrate, by dismissing the petition outright, exercised discretion in an unduly harsh manner, especially when other less drastic alternatives (costs, final warning, day-to-day trial) were available.
32. In State of Punjab v. Shamlal Murari, (1976) 1 SCC 719, it was held that courts must lean in favour of adjudication on merits rather than dismissal on technicalities.

entities.text: State of Punjab v. Shamlal Murari, (1976) 1 SCC 719
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Applying this principle, it is clear that the dismissal order cannot be sustained.

33. It must also be remembered that the proceedings involve not merely the rights of Appellant No.1, but also those of the minor child, Appellant No.2, who is entitled to a safe and secure environment.
34. In Gaurav Nagpal v. Sumedha Nagpal, (2009) 1 SCC 42, the Supreme Court emphasized that in all matrimonial disputes, the welfare of the child is of paramount consideration.

sentences.text: The dismissal of the DV petition has left the minor child without protective orders, exposing her to continued risk.
This is wholly against the principle of welfare of the child.
36. Courts are duty-bound to discourage delay and at the same time prevent miscarriage of justice.
In Bani Singh v. State of U.P., (1996) 4 SCC 720, the Supreme Court held that appeals should not be dismissed for default and must ordinarily be decided on merits.

entities.text: Bani Singh v. State of U.P., (1996) 4 SCC 720
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This principle extends equally to quasi-criminal proceedings like those under the DV Act.
37. Similarly, in K.K. Velusamy v. N. Palanisamy, (2011) 11 SCC 275, it was observed that procedural rules are not to be interpreted as traps but as tools to advance justice.

entities.text: K.K. Velusamy v. N. Palanisamy, (2011) 11 SCC 275

sentences.text: Therefore, this Court is persuaded that restoration is the only just course.
38. The Trial Court failed to appreciate the bona fide difficulties of the appellants.
The dismissal order frustrates the object of the DV Act.
The proportionality of judicial discretion was not maintained.
The rights of the minor child were ignored.
The equities demand restoration subject to imposition of costs to balance inconvenience caused to the respondent.
Accordingly, Point No.1 is answered in the Negative and Point No.2 and 3 are answered in the Affirmative.

39. Point No.4:- In light of my answer to point No.1 to 3, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
The appeal filed by the appellant under Sec.29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is hereby ALLOWED.

 JUDGMENT
The present appeal is directed against the order dated 15.05.2025 passed by the Learned V Metropolitan Magistrate & Traffic Court, Bengaluru in Crl. Misc. No. 23/2024, whereby the petition filed by the appellants under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act,
2005 came to be dismissed for default.
2.
opennyai_summary.facts:
However, on 29.03.2025, since the Trial court was not in session on account of the Presiding Officer being transferred, the matter was adjourned in the same stage.
Hence, the Trial Court erred in dismissing the Petition solely on the ground that 11 adjournments had been sought to adduce evidence, without examining the reasons for those adjournments.
The Trial Court failed to appreciate that the adjournments were not sought with the intent to delay proceedings but were occasioned by genuine circumstances, including the pendency of settlement discussions between the parties in all the connected matrimonial proceedings.
g) Trial Court has failed to appreciate that the counsel was present on all the hearing dates: The appellants through their counsel, have diligently appeared before the trial Court on all previous hearing dates.
On each occasion where an adjournment was sought the factual difficulties faced by appellant No.1 including the on-going settlement talks with the Respondent were duly explained to the Court.
Only upon such explanation being tendered and found to be bona-fide was the matter adjourned in the same stage.
At no point was there any wilful default or negligence on the part of the Appellants in conducting the matter.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The Trial Court has failed to consider the overall conduct of the appellant who has been diligently prosecuting the matter, and the surrounding circumstances.
A mere perusal of the order sheet of the number of adjournments granted could not have provided the entire facts, circumstances and ongoing developments in the entire matrimonial proceedings.
Even assuming there was some delay, the Trial Court could have exercised its discretion more judiciously by issuing a final warning or granting a last opportunity to lead evidence.
The Trial Court thus failed to properly exercise its discretion and to consider the totality of circumstances, including the bona reasons for previous adjournments and the Appellants' continued participation in related proceedings.
This has resulted in manifest prejudice to the Appellants and has caused a grave miscarriage of justice.
Hence, the Impugned Order is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice and equity.
n) In view of the foregoing, it is imperative for the Appellants to be permitted to continue prosecuting the Petition before the Trial Court.
The Impugned Order dismissing the Petition for default, without duly appreciating the bona-fide difficulties faced by the Appellants, has caused grave prejudice to their rights and remedies under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
o) The Appellants have at all times remained willing and ready to lead evidence and have never abandoned or evinced any intention to abandon the proceedings before the Trial Court.
Any adjournments sought were only on account of genuine and compelling circumstances or in the bona fide belief that the matter would be amicably resolved, and not out of negligence or indifference.
q) The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is a beneficial and remedial legislation enacted to protect women from acts of domestic violence and to ensure their safety,
dignity, and economic security.
The impugned order, by categorically dismissing the Petition itself,
frustrates the very intent and spirit of the Act.
r) That the Impugned Order amounts to a miscarriage of justice and must be set aside in the interest of equity, fairness, and the rule of law.
s) The Appellants are now placed in a situation of continued threat and financial insecurity, despite being entitled to statutory protection under the law.
15. Thus, while the Trial Court was right in being concerned with repeated adjournments, it fell into error by failing to balance procedural discipline with substantive justice.
23. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma, (2013) 15 SCC 755, emphasized that courts must interpret the DV Act liberally to extend maximum protection to aggrieved women.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
On the date of the Impugned Order being passed, the Counsel on record for the Appellants had inadvertently noted down the wrong date and could not appear when the matter was taken up, this was the only occasion on which the Appellant counsel could not be present before the Trial Court.
The party must not be penalized or suffer due to the fault of the advocate.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Hence, the Appellant / petitioners pray before this Court to set aside the impugned order dated 15.5.2025 in Crl.Misc.23/2024 passed by the V Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Bengaluru and restore the proceedings to its original place i.e., before the trial court in Crl.Misc.23/2024 by allowing this Criminal Appeal in the interest of justice and equity.
In the DV proceedings, interim relief was initially granted on 09.02.2024 but later vacated on 26.07.2024.
The equities demand restoration subject to imposition of costs to balance inconvenience caused to the respondent.
39. Point No.4:- In light of my answer to point No.1 to 3, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
The appeal filed by the appellant under Sec.29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is hereby ALLOWED.
The impugned order dated 15.05.2025 passed by the Learned V Metropolitan Magistrate & Traffic Court, Bengaluru in Crl. Misc. No. 23/2024 is hereby set aside.
The matter is remanded to the Trial Court with the following specific directions:
a. The Trial Court shall restore Crl. Misc. No. 23/2024 to its original file forthwith.
b. The appellants shall be afforded a final opportunity to file their chief- examination affidavit and adduce evidence within two weeks from the date of first appearance before the Trial Court.
c. The Trial Court shall ensure that all pending interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 3 and 4, etc.) are also considered on merits.
d. The Trial Court shall adopt a strict schedule for cross-examination and final arguments, so that the matter is disposed of expeditiously, preferably within six months.
Costs of Rs. 10,000/- are imposed on the appellants, payable to the Karnataka State Legal Services Authority, as a measure of balancing equities.
opennyai_summary.issue:
9. In light of the rival contentions, the following pivotal points emerge for determination in this appeal:
1.
Whether the Trial Court was justified in dismissing the petition for default on 15.05.2025?
2. Whether the appellants have shown sufficient and bona fide reasons for their inability to lead evidence despite adjournments?
3. Whether the dismissal order frustrates the object of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005?
4. What order?
